Woodfin 5 In addition to the diagnostics developed for dynamic experiments, DARHT has a developing role conducting static experiments in support of the Enhanced Capability for Subcritical Experiments (ECSE) program along with technologies to strengthen the capa- bilities for all NNSA LIAs. Examples include cold or thermionic cathode studies, and A2 presents the unique capability to explore multi-pulse beam–target physics. As the quality and quantity of DARHT data increases, the need for hydro data management is essential to ensure the data be- comes an enduring resource for generations of weapon designers. Combining as-built device information with experiment setup, accelerator tunes, and dynamic data quickly exceeds a terabyte and can rapidly become unmanageable if a careful process is not followed. Data from each experiment must be collated, protected, made searchable, and archived in a user-friendly electronic data management system (EDMS) for current and future use. Enabling Hydrodynamic Measurements in Complex Environments As mission requirements evolve, there is an increasing need for hydro data in complex environments versus the current laboratory environments (standard temperature and pressure, no shock nor g-load, etc.). Complex environments can include dynamic ther- mal events, high g-loads, hostile environments, and a multitude of global security, safety, and surety scenarios. Given the inherent 3D nature of these problems, additional viewing axes are highly desirable. Incorporation of a second downstream transport (DST) region on A2 will enable improved data collection for all these 3D scenarios without the expense of a complete accelerator. Alter- natively, a Scorpius-type machine could be installed as a fully independent third viewing axis with greater capability, but at a more substantial cost. Due to the substantial cost and operational impact, this is a lower priority, long-term option that is not addressed in this strategy. When considering the complete DARHT system of systems, four axes in a plane appears to be the realistic limit for the packaging of the accelerator DST, VCS, and GRC systems onto the DARHT firing point. In conjunction with the packaging issues, the viability of this proposed work depends strongly on the ability to demonstrate workable fragment mitigation technologies within the VCSs for these extremely violent events. Research and development (R&D) of novel armor techniques that maintain and/or increase radio- graphic quality will be essential. Addressing complex environments at DARHT will require the development of new technologies to simulate, mock-up, or reproduce the desired environment during the hydrodynamic experiment. In summary, implementation of the DCX strategy will provide tremendous advancements for DARHT reliability and resilience, will increase the quality and quantity of data generated at DARHT, and will enable hydrodynamic measurements in complex environments, allowing DARHT to remain the nation’s premier hydro data–generating capability for stockpile certification, safety, security, and emerging global security threats for decades into the future. 6 DCX STRATEGY Since 1992, the United States has maintained a moratorium on nuclear explosive testing and remains committed to assuring the safety, security and reliability of our arsenal through a rigorous science-based stockpile stewardship program. —2022 Nuclear Posture Review, United States
